Six months ago, I wrote that Americans were experiencing the Iran war primarily through higher prices, while much of the rest of the world was confronting something more serious: actual shortages of fuel and other critical products.

In “The U.S. Feels Higher Prices While The World Is Facing Fuel Shortages,” I highlighted several pressure points created by the disruption of traffic through the Strait of Hormuz. India was struggling to secure liquefied petroleum gas, or LPG, fertilizer markets were tightening, Europe faced potential shortages of jet fuel and other refined products, and Asian economies were scrambling to replace energy supplies normally sourced from the Persian Gulf.

At the time, the biggest unknown was how long the disruption would last and how successfully global supply chains could adapt. Six months later, the picture is much clearer. Some of the worst fears did not materialize, but that was largely because countries drew down inventories, rerouted supplies over much longer distances, released emergency stocks, reduced consumption, and paid more to keep products moving. The global energy system proved remarkably adaptable, but much of that adaptation came at a substantial cost.

India provided one of the clearest early examples of a physical shortage. The country traditionally sourced about 90% of its imported LPG from the Middle East, leaving it highly exposed when traffic through Hormuz collapsed. The government reduced LPG allocations to industry to protect household cooking-gas supplies, encouraged some users to switch fuels, and took steps to discourage hoarding as Middle Eastern LPG exports plunged.

India and other Asian buyers eventually found replacement supplies, particularly from the United States. U.S. LPG cargoes were redirected toward Asia, but replacing nearby Gulf production with supplies from the U.S. Gulf Coast meant longer voyages and higher transportation costs. By fall, the immediate shortage had eased as imports diversified and Middle Eastern supplies began to recover.

The episode demonstrated both the strength and the weakness of global energy trade. India did not simply run out of cooking gas, because alternative suppliers responded to higher prices. But securing those alternatives required longer supply chains, higher costs, government intervention, and substantial losses by state fuel retailers that continued selling subsidized LPG below market prices. The shortage eased, but the economic cost did not disappear.

Fertilizer was another major concern because the Persian Gulf plays an outsized role in global agriculture. Gulf producers account for a large share of global urea and ammonia exports, while the region is also important to sulfur markets. Sulfur is a critical input for phosphate fertilizer production, so disruptions can spread well beyond the countries that actually produce it.

Those concerns materialized quickly. Urea prices surged after Hormuz traffic was disrupted, and millions of metric tons of Gulf fertilizer exports were temporarily removed from the market. That raised fears that fertilizer shortages could eventually reduce crop yields and push food prices higher.

The outcome has been less severe than initially feared. China increased urea exports, demand moderated after the Northern Hemisphere application season, and nitrogen fertilizer prices retreated from their wartime peaks. Phosphate markets have remained tighter because sulfur shortages continue to constrain production. Instead of one prolonged worldwide fertilizer shortage, the shock migrated through the supply chain as some bottlenecks eased and others persisted.

That distinction is important. Commodity shortages rarely remain static. High prices encourage conservation, attract new suppliers, and change trade flows, but those adjustments take time and usually impose costs somewhere else in the system.

Europe may provide the best example of a feared shortage that largely failed to materialize. In April, the loss of Middle Eastern jet fuel raised concerns that European airlines could face physical shortages during the busy summer travel season. Europe had become increasingly dependent on imported jet fuel as domestic refining capacity declined, leaving it vulnerable to the disruption of Gulf supplies.

Instead, European refiners increased jet fuel production while imports from the United States and West Africa helped replace missing Middle Eastern barrels. Inventories provided an additional cushion, and the summer passed without the severe shortage that some had feared.

But that does not mean Europe escaped the consequences. Jet fuel became considerably more expensive, forcing airlines to absorb higher costs and reconsider routes that no longer made economic sense. The market solved much of the physical shortage through higher prices, alternative supply routes, increased refinery output, and reduced demand.

Natural gas presents a similar story. Europe entered this conflict in a stronger position than it occupied during the 2022 Russian gas crisis because LNG import capacity had expanded and supplies had become more diversified. Nevertheless, higher global gas prices made it more expensive to refill storage. Germany entered November with unusually low storage levels for the beginning of winter, leaving Europe with less margin if the coming winter is particularly cold.

The most important development since April may not be any individual shortage, but what happened to the inventories and spare capacity that normally cushion supply disruptions. Global oil inventories have fallen substantially since the war began despite major releases from emergency reserves.
